Chapter Three: Challenging Comfort and Consumerism
You know, in a world where success is so often measured by what you own, it’s all too easy to get swept up in chasing after more. Just think about it—every day, ads promise we’ll find happiness with the next big purchase, and the pressure to keep up never really lets up, does it? For a lot of folks, even faith can become just another accessory—something that makes life feel good, helps us fit in, or gives a sense of security.
But what happens when following Jesus starts to clash with this constant drive for more?
There’s a group of friends who found themselves wrestling with these exact questions. They’d chosen to live together in an intentional community, but everywhere they looked, there were reminders of what they were “supposed” to have—a bigger house, a fancier car, the latest gadgets. It hit them: their desires weren’t always their own. The world around them was shaping what they wanted, often without them even noticing.
Over time, they realized that the pursuit of comfort could actually become a trap. It dulled their compassion and made it easy to lose sight of what mattered most.
One afternoon, while sorting through piles of donated clothes for a neighborhood giveaway, one of the friends stopped and really looked at all the stuff people had given away. There were bags and boxes overflowing with things—items bought, used a few times, then forgotten. The sheer amount was almost overwhelming. It was one of those moments that makes you stop and think: how much energy and money goes into things that only bring a moment’s satisfaction?
That experience sparked something. The friends decided to try living more simply. They pooled what they had, shared their meals, and made a real effort to buy only what they actually needed. At first, it honestly felt like a sacrifice. Old habits are tough to break, and let's face it, the pull of convenience is strong. But as time went on, they discovered a new kind of freedom. Without the constant urge to get more, they suddenly had space—for deeper friendships, for creativity, and for generosity.
One evening, a neighbor knocked on their door, asking for help with groceries. Instead of seeing it as a hassle, the friends welcomed the chance to share what they had. That’s when it really clicked: abundance isn’t about having more, but about being willing to give. Sharing—whether it was food, time, or just a listening ear—became their quiet way of pushing back against a culture obsessed with scarcity and competition.
As they kept challenging their own assumptions, the friends noticed how often faith gets used to justify comfort. It’s easy to talk about loving others but still live in isolation, or to pray for the poor without ever really meeting them. But real discipleship, they discovered, takes more than good intentions. It means letting go of the things that keep us insulated from the world’s pain.
Most people don’t realize just how much their lives are shaped by what they own. These friends learned that true security doesn’t come from possessions, but from trusting in something bigger. By choosing to live with less, they found themselves more open to the needs of others—and more willing to take risks, all for the sake of love.
The journey wasn’t always smooth. There were moments of doubt, frustration, and sometimes even longing for the comforts they’d left behind. But every step away from consumerism brought them closer to the heart of what it means to follow Jesus. It wasn’t about choosing poverty for its own sake. It was about making room—for community, for generosity, and for real joy.
